summary:
AEGIS is an offline-first crew-health console for long-duration spaceflight, with a companion portal that brings real smartwatch data into it. A crew member completes a guided check-in, sees each signal against their own baseline, receives prioritised next actions, and can prepare a flight-surgeon escalation summary from any screen. AEGIS Link imports an Apple Health export in the browser, streams live heart rate from standard Bluetooth sensors, or pulls JSON from a local bridge — then hands only heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep, and exercise into the console under an explicit, range-checked, opt-in contract that records provenance. Everything runs on-device: no backend, account, or upload.

This matters because distance from Earth removes real-time clinical guidance. Crews must measure, interpret, act, and escalate alone, and the signals that reveal early decline are exactly what wearables already record. AEGIS closes that loop instead of adding another dashboard.
details:
AEGIS is an offline-first crew-health console for long-duration spaceflight, plus AEGIS Link, a wearable portal that feeds it real device data. It is a working web prototype: no install, backend, account, or internet connection is required.

WHAT IT DOES

The console turns a daily self-check-in into an interpretable readiness picture. A crew member records ten signals — heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise, hydration, and radiation — through a guided three-step check-in with measurement coaching and a red-flag symptom screen. AEGIS then shows a readiness score with the signals that drive it, prioritised next actions, and a plain-language status. A body map explains what changes in six physiological systems in spaceflight; a trends view compares each signal with the crew member's own 7/14/30-day baseline; a field guide maps NASA HRP's five hazards to body systems and lays out a four-level escalation ladder. From any screen, the crew can prepare a flight-surgeon summary containing mission context, abnormal signals, current vitals, and comms delay. Four mission environments change the operational context, including Mars transit.

AEGIS Link adds real wearable intake. It imports an Apple Health export (export.zip or export.xml) by streaming and parsing it in the browser; connects to a Bluetooth heart-rate sensor using the standard Heart Rate Service, with live bpm, RR-derived HRV, contact quality, and battery; and can pull JSON from an optional local bridge receiver fed by a phone automation. It then visualises the data: snapshot tiles with personal baselines, a transparent wearable-readiness heuristic, activity rings, trend charts, sleep-stage nights with sleep debt, and workouts.

HOW THE PIECES CONNECT

The portal never writes into the console's record directly. A chosen subset — heart rate, SpO2, sleep, and exercise — is queued as a pending handoff, range-checked, applied once on the console's next load, and recorded as a provenance event. The other six signals stay manual because a watch does not measure them the way the check-in expects. This is a deliberate safety boundary, not a missing feature.

WHY IT MATTERS

Distance from Earth removes real-time clinical guidance. On a Mars transit a crew member cannot wait for a flight surgeon to interpret a reading, and the signals that reveal early decline — sleep debt, resting heart rate, HRV, oxygen saturation — are exactly what wearables already record. AEGIS closes the loop from sensor to decision instead of adding another dashboard. The same loop applies to remote clinics, ships, polar stations, and disaster response.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, chart library, webfont, or CDN; inline SVG charts; Web Bluetooth; DecompressionStream and a streaming XML parser; localStorage; a Python 3 standard-library bridge receiver; headless Chrome for automated verification. The app runs offline from static files.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

A safety-first contract between consumer wearables and a clinical-adjacent record: opt-in mappings, exact JSON preview, range checks, one-shot application, and provenance. Full Apple Health parsing in the browser at realistic scale: a 57 MB / 247,620-record export imports in about half a second with a small memory footprint. Three honest ingestion routes mean the demo works with hardware, without hardware, or from a phone.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Safety (illustrative screening ranges, red-flag escalation, "not a medical device"), explainability (the readiness score shows its components rather than hiding behind a model), privacy (no upload, no account, no analytics), accessibility (large type, keyboard shortcuts, focus-safe dialogs, reduced-motion support, Lighthouse 100), and honesty (Apple Watch's Bluetooth and HealthKit limits are stated in the product, not buried).

AI ASSISTANCE

This project was built with AI assistance. Code, interface copy, the data model, automated tests, and documentation were generated or substantially refactored with DeepSeek (a DeepSeek Harness agent) under human direction, review, and testing. No AI-generated images, audio, or video are included: every screenshot is a real capture of the running application. NASA resources informed the hazard framework and citations; no NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers are used, and the project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. Full disclosure is provided in AI-DISCLOSURE.md in the project repository.

NASA RESOURCES USED

The field guide's five-hazard structure and risk context draw on NASA Human Research Program public resources: the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, the Risks of Human Spaceflight, and the NASA Human Research Program site. These are cited in-app and in the README. No NASA dataset is bundled.
